originalGroup.material:
A. Saturday at Maple School

Saturday at Maple School

Our school is opening its garden to families this Saturday. Come and find out what grows behind the sports hall!

Garden walks start at 9:30 and 11:00. Each walk takes thirty minutes. Meet at the small gate next to the library, not at the main school gate. Students from the gardening club will show visitors the vegetable beds and the new pond. Children must stay with an adult near the pond.

At 10:15, visitors can plant a bean in a paper pot. This activity is free, but there are only twenty places. Please write your name on the list at the garden gate when you arrive. You can take your pot home afterwards.

Bring drinking water and wear shoes that are suitable for walking on grass. There is no café in the garden. If it rains heavily, the garden walks will be cancelled, but the bean activity will move into Room 4 beside the library. Updates will be on the school website by 8:30 on Saturday.

You do not need to book a garden walk. We look forward to seeing you!

B. The smaller sunflower

In April, Leo and his sister Anna each planted a sunflower seed in a pot. Leo put his pot beside the kitchen window. Anna put hers on the balcony. Both children watered their plants, and soon each pot had a small green shoot.

After a few weeks, Anna's plant was taller. Leo looked at his shorter plant and said, 'Maybe I should give it more water.' His grandfather asked whether the soil was dry. It was still wet, so Leo did not add more. Instead, his grandfather suggested checking how much sunlight the plant received. A large tree outside the kitchen kept the window in shade for much of the day.

Leo moved his pot to the balcony. He also turned it a little every few days because the plant leaned towards the light. He did not expect it to become as tall as Anna's immediately. Every Sunday, he measured it and drew a small picture in his notebook.

By July, Leo's plant was still shorter, but both sunflowers had yellow flowers. Anna liked her tall plant. Leo liked looking through his notebook and seeing how his had changed. When a neighbour asked which child had grown the better sunflower, Anna answered, 'We both grew a flower, but Leo grew a whole book about his!'

originalGroup.material:
A. Where to refill a bottle

The Green Street youth club made a map of places where people could refill drinking-water bottles. The first version showed five public taps as blue dots. Club members thought it was clear and simple. Then their neighbour Mr Hall tried to use it on a warm Sunday morning. Two of the taps were inside buildings that were closed.

The members realised that a dot answered 'where' but not 'when'. They visited each place again and asked the staff about opening hours. One sports centre allowed anyone to use its tap, while a small museum let only ticket holders enter the area containing its water point. Both offered drinking water, but they were not equally useful to every passer-by.

The new map gave opening times and explained whether visitors needed a ticket. The club also added a telephone number for reporting changes. It did not publish staff members' personal numbers. If the club received a report, two members checked the information before changing the map.

When a new water point opened at the bus station, the club was careful about its description. The tap was beside the ticket machines, not inside the waiting room. This detail mattered because the waiting room closed at night while the machines remained accessible. The members had learned that useful information often needed more than a mark in the correct place.

B. A repair lesson that began with listening

Before a weekend repair workshop, sixteen-year-old Jamal practised changing a bicycle tyre until he could do it quickly. He expected the younger children to be impressed by his speed. At the workshop, however, most questions were about things he usually did without thinking: which way to hold a tool, how hard to pull, and where to put the small parts.

Jamal began by demonstrating the whole repair while explaining every step. When he asked a child to try, the child could remember only the beginning. Jamal's partner suggested stopping after one small action and letting the learner repeat it before moving on. They also placed tools on a plain tray instead of leaving them in a crowded box.

The lesson became slower, but the children asked more questions. Jamal learned to wait after asking one of his own. If a learner did not answer immediately, he no longer supplied the answer at once. Sometimes the child was simply checking the tyre or choosing words to explain a problem.

At the end, one girl repaired a loose bicycle bell without being shown how to do that particular job. She looked at the tool tray, chose a suitable tool and asked Jamal to check whether the bell was secure. Jamal still valued being able to work quickly himself. But when helping someone else learn, he now cared more about what the other person could do after his hands had moved away.

The Green Street youth club made a map of places where people could refill drinking-water bottles. The first version showed five public taps as blue dots. Club members thought it was clear and simple. Then their neighbour Mr Hall tried to use it on a warm Sunday morning. Two of the taps were inside buildings that were closed.

The members realised that a dot answered 'where' but not 'when'. They visited each place again and asked the staff about opening hours. One sports centre allowed anyone to use its tap, while a small museum let only ticket holders enter the area containing its water point. Both offered drinking water, but they were not equally useful to every passer-by.

The new map gave opening times and explained whether visitors needed a ticket. The club also added a telephone number for reporting changes. It did not publish staff members' personal numbers. If the club received a report, two members checked the information before changing the map.

When a new water point opened at the bus station, the club was careful about its description. The tap was beside the ticket machines, not inside the waiting room. This detail mattered because the waiting room closed at night while the machines remained accessible. The members had learned that useful information often needed more than a mark in the correct place.

options.text: It was reserved for people holding museum tickets.
It was the only place with clean drinking water.
It remained open later than every other water point.
It could be used only by youth-club members.

questions.prompt: What surprised Jamal at the start of the workshop?
questions.material:
B. A repair lesson that began with listening

Before a weekend repair workshop, sixteen-year-old Jamal practised changing a bicycle tyre until he could do it quickly. He expected the younger children to be impressed by his speed. At the workshop, however, most questions were about things he usually did without thinking: which way to hold a tool, how hard to pull, and where to put the small parts.

Jamal began by demonstrating the whole repair while explaining every step. When he asked a child to try, the child could remember only the beginning. Jamal's partner suggested stopping after one small action and letting the learner repeat it before moving on. They also placed tools on a plain tray instead of leaving them in a crowded box.

The lesson became slower, but the children asked more questions. Jamal learned to wait after asking one of his own. If a learner did not answer immediately, he no longer supplied the answer at once. Sometimes the child was simply checking the tyre or choosing words to explain a problem.

At the end, one girl repaired a loose bicycle bell without being shown how to do that particular job. She looked at the tool tray, chose a suitable tool and asked Jamal to check whether the bell was secure. Jamal still valued being able to work quickly himself. But when helping someone else learn, he now cared more about what the other person could do after his hands had moved away.

options.text: The children asked about actions that seemed obvious to him.
No child had ever seen a bicycle before.
The children repaired every bicycle faster than he could.
Every question concerned the price of a new bicycle.

originalGroup.material:
A. A small change at the snack counter

The snack counter at Elm School sold fruit, sandwiches and yoghurt after lessons. On some days, sandwiches sold out within ten minutes. On others, several were left when the counter closed. The staff could not simply prepare more every day, because unsold food would be wasted.

A group of students suggested advance orders. Students could order a sandwich before the end of lunch and collect it after school. The counter would still prepare a smaller number for people who had not ordered. This meant that forgetting to order did not automatically mean going without a snack.

For the first week, the order form asked for a student's name, class, choice and collection time. Staff soon discovered that the collection-time box was not useful: most students wrote 'after school'. They replaced it with a question about food allergies and kept the information available only to the staff preparing the food. The order list was not displayed where other students could read it.

After a month, fewer sandwiches were left over, but the staff did not claim that advance ordering had solved every problem. Fruit was still bought in person, and a rainy afternoon could change how many students stayed after lessons. The system helped with one decision—how many sandwiches to prepare—while leaving room to respond to the day as it happened.

B. The birds that were easy to miss

During a school bird-counting project, Tessa and her friend Owen visited the park every Friday afternoon. They wrote down every bird they could identify and the number they saw. In their first report, they said that one corner of the park had almost no birds.

Their science teacher asked how they had checked that corner. Tessa explained that they usually passed it quickly because it was beside a busy road. The teacher suggested spending the same amount of time in each area. On the next visit, Tessa and Owen stopped there for ten minutes, just as they did beside the pond.

At first they saw nothing. Then a movement in a bush caught Owen's eye. Several small birds were searching for food close to the ground. The birds were less easy to notice than the ducks on the open pond, but they were certainly there. The two students changed their route so that they could observe the corner without standing directly in front of the bush.

They did not erase their earlier records. Instead, they added a note explaining the shorter observation time and marked the week when they had changed their method. Their new report said that the earlier counts could not show whether there had been fewer birds in that corner or simply less chance of noticing them. Tessa found this conclusion less exciting than a clear ranking of the park's best bird areas. She also knew it was more honest about what their observations could tell them.

B. The birds that were easy to miss

During a school bird-counting project, Tessa and her friend Owen visited the park every Friday afternoon. They wrote down every bird they could identify and the number they saw. In their first report, they said that one corner of the park had almost no birds.

Their science teacher asked how they had checked that corner. Tessa explained that they usually passed it quickly because it was beside a busy road. The teacher suggested spending the same amount of time in each area. On the next visit, Tessa and Owen stopped there for ten minutes, just as they did beside the pond.

At first they saw nothing. Then a movement in a bush caught Owen's eye. Several small birds were searching for food close to the ground. The birds were less easy to notice than the ducks on the open pond, but they were certainly there. The two students changed their route so that they could observe the corner without standing directly in front of the bush.

They did not erase their earlier records. Instead, they added a note explaining the shorter observation time and marked the week when they had changed their method. Their new report said that the earlier counts could not show whether there had been fewer birds in that corner or simply less chance of noticing them. Tessa found this conclusion less exciting than a clear ranking of the park's best bird areas. She also knew it was more honest about what their observations could tell them.

options.text: Whether any ducks had been seen near the pond.
Which students had joined the project.
Whether the park was open on Friday afternoons.
Whether low counts reflected fewer birds or a lower chance of seeing them.
